sections.hypothesis: Of btc-regime-trend's three parts (BTC above its 50-day average, the coin up over 30 days, sizing to 50% volatility), the BTC regime filter carries most of its result on ETH and SOL: taking it out lowers the Sharpe after costs more than taking out the coin's own trend, and the volatility sizing changes the risk more than the Sharpe. Information only: which part carries the rule, not a new strategy.
sections.rationale: Every rule must earn its place: a part that adds nothing is complexity with a cost, and a strategy whose result rests on one part is a different claim from one that needs all three (the ablation idea, from a backtesting video Luke shared on 2026-11-26; the method is standard in machine learning). Who pays is unchanged from btc-regime-trend's notes: altcoins follow BTC's regime, and buyers who chase a coin's own trend late. Outside evidence for the parts: time-series momentum (Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen, Journal of Financial Economics 2012) for the coin's trend; volatility-managed portfolios (Moreira and Muir, Journal of Finance 2017) for the sizing. Already known here, and disclosed: on BTC, the sizing alone (vol-hold) scored a Sharpe of 0.93, below holding (findings 2); btc-regime-trend's timing beat 100% of its own weights at random times on ETH and SOL (findings 28). The full rule's runs exist (Sharpe 1.33 on ETH 2020-01 to 2025-10, 1.72 on SOL 2020-08 to 2025-10) and are not rerun. Expected, written before any run: without the BTC filter, Sharpe falls on both coins, the most of any change; without the coin trend, it falls less; fully in instead of sized, the Sharpe is about the same and the drawdown deeper; with both filters off (vol-hold), the Sharpe is close to holding's. This never changes a running strategy: the holdout is spent for ETH and SOL, so no variant could be validated, and the paper accounts keep the full rule. Not a rejected family.
sections.rules: Implementation btc-regime-ablation (kestrel.strategies.btc_regime.BtcRegimeAblation): btc-regime-trend with each part switchable; with every switch on it is btc-regime-trend exactly (a test checks this), and every variant waits for the full rule's warm-up so all are compared over the same days. Daily bars, spot, long only, 330 USDT, costs from kestrel.toml. ETHUSDT 2020-01 to 2025-10 and SOLUSDT 2020-08 to 2025-10, as the full rule's runs. For each coin, four backtests (kestrel backtest <COIN> --interval 1d --start <first> --end 2025-10 --research <this note> --param ...): (a) btc_filter=0; (b) coin_trend=0; (c) vol_sizing=0; (d) btc_filter=0 coin_trend=0 (vol-hold). Every other setting at its default. Then kestrel random-timing on each variant (a control, not a trial). Nothing before the holdout's start is excluded and nothing after it is read.
sections.falsification: Information only: there is no pass or fail, and no decision changes. The hypothesis is wrong if, on both coins, taking out the coin trend lowers the Sharpe more than taking out the BTC filter. Reported for each variant beside the full rule: Sharpe after costs, its exposure-matched holding (test 1), max drawdown, exposure, trades, and the random-timing share. A part 'earns its place' on a coin when removing it lowers the Sharpe by more than 0.1; smaller differences are reported as no clear difference (a Sharpe's sampling error over five years is several times that, so even 0.1 is a reading, not proof).
sections.parameters: The defaults (btc_days 50, coin_days 30, vol_days 30, target_vol_pct 50) throughout; only the three switches change, in the four combinations above. Nothing else is run.
sections.costs: kestrel.toml's costs, as every run. Trials: 8 backtests in the crypto pool (four variants on two coins), which raise the luck bar slightly; the random-timing controls are not trials.
